title: Estimating a Launch (Judge the Launch Game)
objectives: Judge a launch on float, cliff length, and insider share instead of unit price
Compare an FDV against real sector peers and ask whether the multiple makes sense
Run a four-point checklist that separates a fair launch from an insider exit

steps.title: Day 1 Euphoria vs. Fundamental Reality
steps.body:
When a hyped project launches a token on Solana, the volume is real. Millions of dollars move through Jupiter in the first hours, and social feeds fill with price targets.

Traders who have been through a few launches look at something else entirely. Not the unit price — $0.50 versus $5.00 tells you nothing on its own — but the float ratio, the <Term id="fdv">FDV</Term>, and the countdown until early backers can sell.

Retail watches the ticker. The rest of us read the supply schedule and the <Term id="vesting">vesting</Term> contracts.

steps.title: The 'Low Float, High FDV' Playbook
steps.body:
You have met this pattern before in I9. It is worth walking through with real numbers, because it is still the most common way launch buyers lose.

1. **Artificial scarcity.** A protocol issues 1,000,000,000 tokens and unlocks only 2% to 5% on day one — say 30M tokens.
2. **Inflated price.** With very few tokens available, modest buying pushes the price to $2.00 and an initial <Term id="market_cap">market cap</Term> of $60M. That looks reasonable.
3. **Hidden giant.** At $2.00 the <Term id="fdv">FDV</Term> is $2 billion — higher than established blue-chip protocols doing hundreds of millions in real fee volume.
4. **The inevitable bleed.** The remaining 95% unlocks over the next two years. Secondary market liquidity gets overwhelmed, and the token bleeds 80% to 95% against SOL.

You do not need to predict which projects will do this. You need to notice that the <Term id="float">float</Term> is tiny before you buy.

steps.title: Benchmarking with Sector Peers ('Comps')
steps.body:
Traditional analysts value companies against comparable companies. The same discipline applies to DeFi tokens, and it is the fastest check you can run.

- If established Solana DEXs trade at an FDV of $400M to $600M while processing billions in monthly volume, does a brand new swap router deserve a $1.5B FDV on day one?
- If a perpetuals DEX generates $100k a year in protocol fees, is a 1,000x fee multiple justifiable?

When a newly launched token's FDV exceeds that of a sector leader with ten times the users and revenue, it is not 'early'. It is mispriced relative to everything already working.

steps.title: The 4-Pillar Due Diligence Checklist
steps.body:
Before buying any newly launched token, check four things:

1. **Circulating float: 15% or more.** Enough supply that early market makers cannot monopolise and squeeze the price.
2. **Relative peer multiple: 2.5x or less.** The <Term id="fdv">FDV</Term> should not exceed roughly 2.5 times the median of battle-tested peers in the same niche.
3. **Lockup <Term id="cliff">cliff</Term>: 12 months or more.** Retail buyers get protected through the critical build phase instead of funding early investors' exit.
4. **Insider share: 35% or less.** The community, liquidity providers, and DAO control the true majority of long-term supply.

Miss one and you are taking a bigger swing than the pitch suggests. Miss two and you are probably the exit liquidity.

steps.title: Under the Hood: Market Maker Call Options & Loans
steps.body:
Behind almost every major token launch sits a market-making deal that is rarely written in the whitepaper.

The structure: the protocol loans tens of millions of tokens to a high-frequency trading firm alongside European-style call options. The market maker uses those loaned tokens to provide depth on DEX pools while hedging on centralized exchanges, and the options give it the right — not the obligation — to buy at a fixed price later.

This explains behaviour you will otherwise find confusing:

- Launch prices often hover in tight corridors for weeks. That is the market maker defending a band, not organic price discovery.
- Liquidity can look deep and then thin out quickly once the loan term ends.
- As option expiries approach, the incentive to hedge and dump increases, which is one reason early launch highs fade.

None of this is illegal, and none of it is automatically a red flag. But a deal that gives a professional firm cheap tokens and a free option means the early chart is not a clean read on demand. Read the loan terms when they are disclosed, and assume they exist when they are not.

questions.prompt: What is the primary danger of a token that launches with only 3% circulating supply and a $2B FDV?
options: The Solana blockchain will fail to process transactions
The 97% locked supply will inevitably dilute holders as massive unlock waves hit secondary liquidity
Holders will be forced to pay 97% tax on every swap
The smart contract cannot be audited
questions.explainRight: A 3% float means 97% of the supply is still locked and has to arrive eventually. Unlock waves of that size almost always overwhelm buy pressure, so early holders get diluted relentlessly. The small market cap is an illusion created by hiding most of the pizza in the kitchen.
questions.explainWrong: The danger is not technical and there is no tax. It is supply: the 97% locked today is future sell pressure that will hit secondary markets as lockups expire, which is exactly what the low-float trap does to late buyers.

questions.prompt: If established, battle-tested lending protocols in an ecosystem trade at a $100M FDV, what should you conclude if a brand new unproven lending fork launches at $800M FDV?
options: It is a bargain because the number is bigger
It is heavily overvalued relative to comps and likely to face severe valuation repricing
The token must have 8x more smart contract code
The validators have pre-approved the $800M valuation
questions.explainRight: Comps matter. If seasoned lending protocols with years of uptime and real revenue sit at a $100M FDV, an unproven fork at $800M is asking eight times the valuation with none of the track record. Repricing risk is severe, and you are paying for narrative rather than fees.
questions.explainWrong: A bigger number is not a better deal, validators do not pre-approve valuations, and more code does not create more value. When a newcomer is priced far above sector leaders without proven traction, the market is simply early to the correction.

questions.prompt: Which of the following launch structures represents the healthiest balance for retail market participants?
options: 25% float, 12-month investor cliff with linear vesting, 25% insider allocation
0.5% float, no cliff, 90% venture capital allocation
50% float with 100% unlocked for the team on Day 1
questions.explainRight: A quarter of supply circulating on day one, a full year cliff followed by linear vesting, and only a quarter held by insiders. Retail has real liquidity to trade, insiders are locked through the build phase, and the community controls most of the supply.
questions.explainWrong: The other structures concentrate risk in different ways: 2% float with a 3-month cliff and 70% insiders is an exit plan; 0.5% with no cliff is worse; full day-one team unlock invites an instant dump. A healthy launch combines float above roughly 15% to 20%, cliffs of at least 12 months, and insider control under about 35%.
